title: SRE SLOs, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, and Runbook Standards
author: Ari Chen
summary: Standards and playbooks for defining SLOs and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review requirements, operational tooling expectations, and SRE runbook structure.
content:
Overview

This document captures Redwood Inference's SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling expectations, and the canonical runbook format. It is intended as the single source of truth for teams operating production services and for on-call engineers managing incidents.

Key goals
- Provide clear, measurable SLOs for all externally and internally visible services.
- Standardize error budget policy and automatic/manual escalation procedures.
- Define a repeatable capacity planning process tied to business metrics and forecast windows.
- Align incident review and postmortem expectations to drive continuous improvement.
- Specify tooling and dashboards required for effective on-call and runbook execution.

Scope and applicability
- Applies to all services owned by eng-* teams serving production inference traffic (hosted API, routing, runtime, telemetry, billing, control plane).
- Core infra services (redis, postgres, kafka, model-serving runtime) must have SLOs defined and onboarded to the SRE dashboard.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

1.1 SLO definitions (recommended templates)
- Availability SLO (user-visible): percent of successful requests (HTTP 2xx/streaming success) over a rolling 30d window. Example: 99.95% availability for Redwood-API (public inference).
- Latency SLOs (p95/p99): request end-to-end latency measured at the API gateway or edge. Examples: p95 < 150ms, p99 < 400ms for small requests (<=512 tokens).
- Correctness SLO (optional): successful response format / schema validation for structured outputs (e.g., function-calling). Example: 99.9% schema-valid responses over 30d.
- Background/Batch SLOs: throughput or completion-time targets for bulk jobs (e.g., nightly embedding batch must complete within 3 hours).

1.2 Measurement windows and error budget calculation
- Default rolling window: 30 days (secondary window: 7d for alerting).
- Error budget = (1 - SLO) * window_capacity; express in % of requests or token-ops.
- Example: For 99.95% SLO, monthly error budget = 0.05% of total requests.

1.3 Alerting and signal sources
- Primary signal: production telemetry pipeline (Prometheus-derived metrics from service sidecars + gateway metrics).
- Secondary signals: synthetic checks (global canaries), tracing-derived latency, and user-facing SLA-alerting from the edge.
- Alert thresholds (baseline):
  - SEV-1 (page): SLO burn > 20% within 1h OR availability drop > 1% absolute within 15m.
  - SEV-2 (page on-call, notify secondary): sustained SLO burn > 10% over 6h OR p99 latency > 2x target for 10m.
  - SEV-3 (ticket): warning: error budget consumption > 25% over 7d (requires review at weekly reliability meeting).

1.4 Error budget policy (actions on burn)
- Tier 1: < 25% budget used — monitor, schedule reliability improvements in normal cadence.
- Tier 2: 25%–50% — pause non-essential feature launches that would increase load on the service; required triage and mitigation plan within 48h.
- Tier 3: 50%–75% — mandatory reliability initiative (see §3), prioritize mitigations, increased monitoring and runbook drills; SR owner required.
- Tier 4: >75% — emergency mitigation: rollback risky changes, enable throttles/rate-limits, alert execs and product; require incident review within 72h and a blocking task in the product backlog until error budget is replenished.

1.5 Ownership and SLO reviews
- Each SLO must list an owner (team lead) and a secondary on the SLO definition page. SLOs are reviewed quarterly or on major architecture changes.

2) Capacity Planning

2.1 Principles
- Capacity is planned against both request throughput and tail latency constraints (latency-sensitive workloads must have headroom for traffic spikes).
- Use a forecast horizon with three buckets: short-term (0–3 months), medium (3–12 months), long-term (12+ months).
- Tie capacity forecasts to business signals (MAU, paid customer commits, upcoming marketing campaigns, model release pages).

2.2 Data sources and inputs
- Telemetry: 95/99/mean RPS, token-per-request distribution, p50/p95/p99 latencies, CPU/GPU utilization, IO metrics.
- Business: sales forecast, committed Reserved capacity (Dedicated customers), launch calendar.
- Experiments: model changes (bigger models -> higher tokens/compute per request).

2.3 Forecasting method (recommended)
1. Baseline: use last 90 days' rolling average RPS and tokens-per-request distribution.
2. Apply growth factors from business input (e.g., +20% due to sales commit A).
3. Estimate capacity per instance type: tokens/sec per GPU, steady-state batch efficiency, and quantization profile adjustments.
4. Add safety margin: latency-sensitive services require 40% headroom; background jobs 20% headroom.
5. Convert to procurement plan: number of GPUs and expected procurement/lease lead time.

2.4 Operational checklist for capacity changes
- Run load-testing against canary cluster; verify p99 latency and GPU utilization.
- Update autoscaling policies and burst pools.
- Schedule maintenance windows with CS and sales for Dedicated customers where applicable.
- Post-deploy: validate synthetic checks and production telemetry for 48h before marking capacity as live.

3) Reliability Initiatives and Prioritization

3.1 Initiative categories
- Observability improvements: dashboards, SLO coverage, tracing sampling.
- Performance: kernel/compilation improvements, batching, caching.
- Resiliency: fallbacks, circuit breakers, regional routing.
- Cost/stability tradeoffs: quantization or model variant rollouts with controlled canaries.

3.2 Prioritization rubric
- Impact on SLO/revenue (high/med/low).
- Effort estimate (person-weeks).
- Cross-team dependencies.
- Priority = Impact / Effort, with executive alignment for infra-wide initiatives.

3.3 Example initiatives (Q2–Q3 cadence)
- Reduce p99 inference latency by 15% via improved KV cache eviction and batching window tuning (owner: eng-serving-runtime).
- Add cross-region canaries with synthetic traffic to detect regressions in <5m (owner: eng-platform).

4) Incident Review Standards (Postmortems)

4.1 Required elements for every Sev-1/SEV-2 postmortem
- Title, incident start/end timestamps, severity, services impacted, customer impact summary.
- Timeline of events (minute-granular for SEV-1).
- Root cause analysis (technical), contributing factors, detection path, mitigation steps taken.
- Quantitative impact: requests lost, latency degradation, error budget consumed.
- Action items with owners and due dates (SMART: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound).
- Blameless language and focus on systems/processes.

4.2 Postmortem timeline and SLAs
- Initial incident report: within 12 hours of mitigation.
- Full draft postmortem: within 72 hours.
- Final postmortem published and assigned action items tracked: within 14 days.
- Follow-up review: 30/90 day check-in on action item completion.

5) Operational Tooling and Dashboards

5.1 Minimum dashboard set per service (must exist before service considered production-ready)
- SLO overview (30d, 7d windows) with error budget burn graph.
- Key latency histograms (p50/p95/p99), request rate, token-rate.
- Resource utilization: GPU utilization, mem, disk IO for stateful components.
- Alerts panel: active alerts by severity and last 24h alert count.

5.2 Required tooling and integrations
- Metrics: Prometheus + Cortex for long-term retention.
- Tracing: Jaeger/Tempo with 1% sampling by default; increase for canaries.
- Synthetic checks: global canaries (us-east-1, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1) using production model variants.
- On-call: PagerDuty integration with escalation policies aligned with SEV definitions.
- Runbook storage: canonical runbooks must live in the runbooks repo (git URL: git@repo.redwood.internal:sre/runbooks) and be referenced in the service page.

5.3 Example Prometheus alert (stringified example)
- ALERT ServiceHighP99Latency
  IF histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le)) > 0.4
  FOR 10m
  LABELS { severity="page" }

6) Runbook Standards and Template

6.1 Runbook structure (required fields)
- Title (service-name / action)
- Summary: one-line description of purpose and when to run.
- Owner and secondary contact (PagerDuty rotation).
- Preconditions: required tooling, log locations, runbook prerequisites.
- Detection indicators: alerts and dashboard panels that map to this runbook.
- Step-by-step remediation (numbered), with clear commands and expected outcomes.
- Rollback steps and verification commands.
- Post-incident checks and follow-up actions.
- Links: architecture diagrams, SLO page, related runbooks, postmortem template.

6.2 Example (excerpt)
- Title: "API Gateway: Throttle misbehaving clients"
- Summary: "Use to mitigate client-driven surges causing p99 latency degradation."
- Owner: eng-platform (oncall: gateway-team)
- Preconditions: admin access to gateway-control-plane, PagerDuty acknowledged.
- Steps:
  1. Identify offending client by querying gateway logs: `kubectl -n gateway logs -l app=gateway | grep "client_id" | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head`
  2. Apply temporary throttle: `gatewayctl throttle client --id <client_id> --rate 10rps --duration 1h`
  3. Monitor p99 latency and error budget dashboard for 10m.
  4. If stable, set a 24h limit and open a ticket with CS to engage the customer.
  Rollback: `gatewayctl throttle client --id <client_id> --remove`

7) Governance, Reviews, and Exceptions
- Quarterly SLO review meetings (owners present) to validate SLOs, thresholds, and measurement fidelity.
- Any exception to error budget policy must be documented with a business justification, labeled, and approved by SRE lead + product.

8) Templates and Artifacts (links)
- SLO definition template: git@repo.redwood.internal:infra/slo-templates/standard-slo.md
- Runbooks repo: git@repo.redwood.internal:sre/runbooks
- Postmortem template: /confluence/templates/postmortem-template.md

Appendix A — Example SLO table (example values)\n
| Service | SLO (30d) | Primary metric | Owner | Alert window | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| Redwood-API (public) | 99.95% availability | successful_requests/total | eng-api | 1h | p95 < 150ms |
| Runtime Inference (small models) | p95 < 150ms / p99 < 400ms | latency at gateway | eng-serving-runtime | 10m | measured at 512 token requests |
| Embedding Batch | 99% completion / 24h | job_success/total | eng-platform | 24h | nightly window |

Appendix B — Error budget escalation checklist (actionable)
1. Owner notified and acknowledges within 1h.
2. Triage call if burn is Tier 3+ (video/audio channel + notes).
3. Apply mitigations (rate-limits, increased capacity, rollback).
4. Publish status update on internal status page and notify customer-facing teams.
5. Post-incident review and SLO recalibration if necessary.
